title: India Unlikely to Face Food or Fertiliser Crisis Despite Global Headwinds, Says Panagariya
excerpt: The 16th Finance Commission chairman told ANI that strengthened fertiliser supplies and India's proven ability to absorb energy shocks mean the country need not fear the global food crisis Jaishankar warned of.
body:
• India is unlikely to face a major food or fertiliser crisis despite continuing global conflicts, 16th Finance Commission Chairman Arvind Panagariya said on Saturday.
  • Speaking to ANI at the 5th Kautilya Economic Conclave in New Delhi, Panagariya said India's fertiliser position had strengthened — partly through restarted domestic plants — and that supplies could be sourced from other countries.
  • His assessment was a direct response to External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar's warning earlier this week that Ukraine and West Asia conflicts were straining grain exports and fertiliser production, with a major food crisis possible in the coming months.
  • Indian households remain insulated so far, Panagariya said: the energy shock's impact on households was limited, with only commercial LPG users such as restaurants and hotels facing temporary pressure.

India is unlikely to face a major food or fertiliser crisis despite continuing global conflicts, 16th Finance Commission Chairman Arvind Panagariya said on Saturday, pointing to strengthened fertiliser supplies and the country's demonstrated ability to absorb energy shocks.

Speaking to news agency ANI on the sidelines of the 5th Kautilya Economic Conclave in New Delhi, Panagariya was responding to External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar's warning earlier this week that pressures from the Ukraine and West Asia conflicts were affecting grain exports and fertiliser production, while energy costs and tighter financial conditions added strain on developing economies.

Context & Background

Jaishankar's warning, delivered days earlier, framed the risk in stark terms: disruptions to Black Sea shipping were keeping major grain exporters from reaching global markets, fertiliser shortages were already significant, and a major food crisis could arrive "in the coming months" unless governments acted responsibly.

Panagariya's rebuttal drew on recent Indian experience. "If we look at our recent experience with the war in West Asia and the way we were able to handle the energy side, I do not think there is anything here that we need to fear very seriously," he said. The government has said it maintained adequate fertiliser availability through West Asia-related supply disruptions via domestic production, diversified imports and advance stocking.

"If we look at our recent experience with the war in West Asia and the way we were able to handle the energy side, I do not think there is anything here that we need to fear very seriously."

— Arvind Panagariya, Chairman, 16th Finance Commission

Impact & Analysis

The contrast between Jaishankar's global alarm and Panagariya's domestic calm captures India's two-track positioning: a voice warning of systemic risk for vulnerable economies abroad, and a domestic policy apparatus confident in its buffers at home. The fertiliser arithmetic matters — India is among the world's largest importers of fertiliser inputs such as urea, ammonia and DAP, so a supply crunch would land directly on farm economics. Panagariya's case is that restarted domestic plants plus diversified sourcing have changed that equation. "There is supply, and fertilisers can also be purchased from other countries," he said.

Household insulation is the other pillar. India absorbed the recent energy shock without the inflation spiral or fuel queues seen elsewhere, Panagariya argued — "We were able to absorb this shock quite well. Going forward, I believe our ability to absorb such shocks will increase, not decrease" — with only commercial LPG users such as restaurants and hotels facing temporary pressure. "Every economy faces some shocks," he added, noting India had previously absorbed far larger disruptions such as the Covid pandemic and the banking system's bad-loan crisis.

On the growth front, Panagariya remained positive after real GDP expanded 7.8 per cent in the April-June quarter of FY27, saying annual growth could stay at least 7 per cent "for some time to come" and pointing to the manufacturing pickup as encouraging. He also turned the disruption argument on its head for Indian agriculture: as a food exporter, India could benefit if the war cut Ukrainian supplies. "If the war leads to lower supplies from Ukraine, demand for our food products could increase. If that pushes prices higher, our exporters would benefit."

Diaspora Angle

For the diaspora, the exchange is a window into how New Delhi calibrates risk. NRIs watching from the Gulf or the West get two signals: the External Affairs Minister pressing for global responsibility on food and fertiliser security, and the Finance Commission chief insisting India's own granaries and fertiliser pipelines are secure. For diaspora investors in agri and food businesses, Panagariya's message is the reassuring one — no domestic supply shock is in view.

What's Next

Whether Panagariya's confidence holds depends on the West Asia conflict's trajectory, winter energy prices and the rabi sowing season's fertiliser demand. Jaishankar's global warning still stands for the world's most vulnerable importers — the question is whether India's buffers stay as thick as the Finance Commission chairman says they are.
